title: Great Hymn to Shamash (Babylonian hymn to the sun god)
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L III.4, Great Prayer to Shamash (ed. G. Rozzi), SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: The Great Hymn to Shamash, hymn: 200 of 200 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (11 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The hymn praises Shamash, whose light illuminates heaven and earth, who watches over all peoples and creatures, judges the dishonest judge, the false merchant and the oppressor, rewards the honest, and hears the prayers of the weak and of travellers on land and sea.

The Great Hymn to Shamash is a Babylonian hymn of about 200 lines to the sun god as the judge who sees everything under heaven and the protector of travellers, merchants, the poor and the oppressed. It survives mainly on copies from the libraries of Nineveh and from Babylonian cities. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/3/4/SB/-) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so (BM.35077, BM.36296). The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 200 of the 200 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 11 tablets in the British Museum: BM.36296, BM.98732 (Nineveh), K.3182 (Nineveh), Sm.1033 (Nineveh), K.3474 (Nineveh), K.3650 (Nineveh), BM.35077, BM.38849, 1883,0118.472 (Nineveh), BM.134517 (Nineveh), BM.98631 (Nineveh).
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; * collated sign; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; < > sign omitted by the scribe, supplied by the editor; << >> sign written in error by the scribe; @v and similar: variant or modified form of a sign; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet; (blank space) a space left by the scribe.

translation.original_ref: BM.36296, obverse, lines 6 to 11 of the tablet = SB 1-6
translation.original_text:
1muš-na-mir gi-mil-lu ka-la-mu
2mu-šah-li ek-le-tu₄ (written over an erasure) a-na UN-MEŠ e-liš u šap-liš
3{d}UTU muš!-na-mir gi-mil-lu ka-la-mu
4mu-šah-li ek-le-tu₄ a-na UN-MEŠ# e-liš u šap-liš
5sah-pu ki-ma šu-uš-kal-lu₄ KI-ti₃! <<ana>> ša₂-ru-ru-ka
6ša₂# hur-sa-a-ni be₂-ru-tu e-ṭ[u-t]i-šu#-nu# tuš#-par#-di#
translation.text:
1Illuminator of the whole of heaven,
2Who makes light the darkness for the peoples, above and below,
3Shamash, illuminator of the whole of heaven,
4Who makes light the darkness for the peoples, above and below,
5Your radiance spreads out like a net over the world,
6You brighten the gloom of the distant mountains.
translation.scan_note: British Museum BM.36296: obverse, the tablet's own lines 6 to 11. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/3/4/SB/-) attributes SB 1-6 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges, with about 13 lines on the obverse and 12 on the reverse, well above eBL's 7 obverse lines. Ink numbers 36296 and 80-6-17,22 are on the edges, and a joined piece at the right is marked 38070 (join line visible). eBL classes BM.36296 as a school tablet (a scribal exercise that copies an excerpt of the text), not a library copy of the whole work. It carries these lines as text (eBL's transliteration has no commentary or quotation markup), and it is used because no photographed library copy preserves these lines as well. On this tablet line 6 is partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of this line translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken. Lines 1-5 are complete on this tablet.

translation.text:
9Your beams unerringly provide the clue to secret places,
10At the brightness of your rising people’s footprints are revealed.
11Your dazzle seeks out [the heavens],
12The four world regions [are warmed up], as if with fire.
13You open up the gates of every [sanctuary],
14You [regulate] the food offerings of the Igigi-gods.
15O Shamash, humankind kneels to your rising,
16All lands bestir themselves towards your light.

17Illuminator of darkness, opener of the bosom of heaven,
18Hastener of the breeze of morn towards the grain fields, life of the land,
19Your splendor envelops the distant mountains,
20Your brilliance fills all the lands.
21Leaning over the mountains, you inspect the earth,
22In heaven, you hold the disk of the world in balance.
23You make the people of all lands your charge,
24Those that Ea, sovereign of kings, has created are wholly entrusted to you.

translation.text:
25You shepherd all living creatures together,
26You are their herdsman, those above and below.
27You cross regularly through the heavens,
28Every day you traverse the vast earth.
29High seas, mountains, earth, and sky,
30You traverse them regularly, every day, as if they were pavement.
31In the lower regions you take charge of the netherworld gods, the demons, the Anunna-gods,
32In the upper regions you administer all the inhabited world.
33Shepherd of the lower regions, herdsman of the upper regions,
34You, Shamash, administer the light for all.
35You cross regularly the wide expanse of the seas,
36[Whose] depths not even the Igigi-gods know.
37O Shamash, your radiance goes down to the deep,
38[The mons]ters of the ocean can see your light.
39You bind mountains together like a cord, you blanket (them) like a haze,
40Your [bro]ad protection is cast over the lands.
41Though your face fall each day, never is it wholly eclipsed,

translation.text:
42At night you are still there, you light up [the darkness].
43To far-off regions unknown and for countless leagues
44You persevere, O Shamash, what you went by day you come back at night.
45Among all the Igigi-gods there is none who does such wearisome toil but you,
46Nor among the gods of the entire universe is one who does so much as you!
47At your rising the gods of the land assemble,
48While your fierce glare covers the land.
49Of all the lands of different tongues,
50[You] know their intentions, you can see their footprints.
51All humankind kneels before you,
52[O Sha]mash, everyone longs for your light,
53At the diviner’s bowl, at the knotted sprigs of cedar,
54At the roasting pot (of offerings set out) by the dream interpreter, who explains visions of the night,
55[Those who are preparing for] rites kneel before you.
56[Be]fore you kneel both wicked and just.
57[Who] goes down to the depths but you?
58You clear up the case of the innocent truth-teller and (his) opponent,

59You give short shrift to the wicked,
60Sleep drifts over the just, so that he breathes as serenely as a sound sleeper.
61You turn back the rogue who restrains [his friend],
62You rescue from the brink of hell those tied up in a lawsuit, [you clear their cause].
63Whatever you say [to them (scil. humankind)] in just verdict, O Shamash,
64Your utterances are manifest, they cannot be changed, [you show] no favoritism.
65You give support to the traveler whose j[ourney] is trying,
66To the seafarer in dread of the waves you grant [courage],
67You escort the roamer on unexplored routes,
68You keep guiding on the trail any who turn toward the sun.
69You rescue from the flashflood the [mer]chant bearing (his) purse,
70You bring up the one gone down to the deep, you set wings (upon him).

85He who shows no respect for an oath by you […],
86For the one who does not revere the invocation of your name, testified in false words,
87Your net is spread, a snare in the earth, a hunting trap indeed!
88The man who co[vets] his neighbor’s wife,
89Death cuts short his lifespan before his destined time,
90A spring is set for him, that vicious man will [step into it],
91Your weapon makes straight for him, he will have none to save him.
92[His] father will not attend his trial,
93Nor will his own brothers reply to the judge’s queries,
94He is caught unawares in a trap of bronze!
95You blunt the horns of the contriver of offenses,
96The swindler plotting to work a draw, his foothold’s undercut.
97You show the roguish judge the (inside of) a jail,
98He who takes the fee but does not carry through, you make him bear the punishment.
99The one who receives no fee but takes up the cause of the weak,
100Shamash is pleased with him, he will prolong his life.
101The scrupulous judge who gives just verdicts,
102He will have a palace at his disposal, princely will be his dwelling.
103What return will there be for the exploitive lender of money?
104He will cause a decrease in profit and he will lose the principal.
105He who invests long-term, who returns one shekel for thr[ee],
106Shamash is pleased with him, he will prolong his life.
107He who cheats as he holds the scales,

109He will cause a decrease in profit and he will lose the principal.
110The one who holds the balance honestly, many are [his …],
111However much (he weighs) will be given to him [sevenfold].

116His first-born son shall not take over his property,
117His own brothers shall not succeed to his estate.
118The honest creditor who makes loans by the [large] standard, he does extra good.

136The shepherd in dread of the wilderness turns to you,
137The herdsman in trouble, the keeper of sheep among the enemy.
138O Shamash, there turns to you the caravan passing through danger,
139The travelling merchant, the agent carrying (his) purse.
140O Shamash, there turns to you the fisherman with his net,
141The hunter, the beater, the one who drives the game,
142The fowler among (his) snares turns to you,
143The footpad, the robber are prayerful to the Sun,
144The bandit on the wilderness tracks turn to you,
145The wandering dead, the vagrant spirit turn to you.
146O Shamash, you have listened to them all,
147You did not deny those who turned to you, but bestowed generously (on them).
148For my sake, O Shamash, do not despise these people!
149You have opened wisdom, O Shamash, to the world,
150You yourself grant people who seek you your fierce and burning light.
151You set straight their omens, you preside over sacrifices.
152You probe their future to the four cardinal points,
153You have opened wisdom to the entire inhabited world.
154The heavens are too puny to be the cup of your gazing,
155All the lands are too puny to be (your) seer’s bowl.
156On the twentieth of the month you rejoice with mirth and joy,
157You dine, you drink their fine brew, the brewer’s beer at wharf side
158They pour out barkeep’s beer for you, you accept it.

translation.text:
180Who can shorten days, who can prolong nights
181Who covers (the earth) with cold, frost, ice, (and) snow,
182Who opens the gate (and) the bolt of heaven, opens wide the doors of the inhabited world,
183Who lifts the socket, the pin, the latchkey, the bolt,
184Who shrivels the relentless, who bestows life,
185[Who ... ] ... the captive in combat, a fight to the death.
186[… rea]son, counsel, deliberation, advice,
187[Who lights the] torch of daybreak, glowing for the people.
188[Who upholds …] scepter, throne, rule, (and) dynasty,
189None among the Igigi can rival your strength.
190May Anu, Enlil, and Ea glorify your [name],
191[…] the fifty [Anunna-gods …],
192May [Be]let-ili, who created the gods, [extend] your dominion.
193[In] radiant [Ebabb]ar, your splendid abode,
194[…] … a banquet from the four world regions.
195[May king, gover]nor, high priest, and prince,
196[…] before you, may they bring you their tribute.
197[…] Ebabbar, in offerings, the yield of the lands,
198[…] in the land, may your throne dais be ever renewed,
199[…] whose utterance cannot be changed,
200[May A]ya, the great bride, say to you in the bedchamber, “Rest!”

Photograph checked: the obverse has two columns in small script, about 40 to 45 and about 27 lines. On the reverse, a joined piece marked K.8233 sits across a column ruling with about 9 lines on each side, and an upper piece has about 12 lines in the left column. This fits eBL's i 42, ii 27, iii 10, iv 22. Ink K.3474 and S.372 are on the edges. On this tablet line 192 is entirely broken, of lines 190-191 only one to three signs survive and lines 180-189, 193-200 are partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian).
